question: Should the United States drop its rule that raw-milk cheese must age at least 60 days before sale?
answer: The rule dates from 1949 and rests on 1940s evidence, chiefly typhoid bacteria dying out in aged cheddar. A 2010 study found E. coli O157 still detectable in raw-milk Gouda and cheddar after 270 days, so ageing gives false comfort while banning young raw-milk cheeses outright. Safety should come from testing milk and inspecting dairies.
move: Whichever side you took, whether ageing or testing better controls the risk decides it.
ask: Is there a rule I follow that was made long ago, for a different time?
counterpoint: The 60-day rule keeps off the shelf exactly the cheeses that carry most risk. A 2015 FDA and Health Canada assessment put the listeriosis risk from raw-milk soft-ripened cheese at 50 to 160 times that of pasteurised versions. Listeria strikes pregnant women and the elderly hardest. An imperfect barrier still blocks the worst category.
source: FDA and Health Canada risk assessment, 2015
